problem: A branch office has 200 employee laptops, phones, and printers, but the ISP has only handed out a single public IPv4 address. IPv4 addresses are a genuinely scarce, exhausted resource — there simply are not enough public addresses in existence to give every device in every company its own. The company cannot ask every device to share one literal IP address and still have them all reach the internet independently and get their replies back correctly.

At the same time, a data center team is migrating a web application that was originally deployed with private addressing, and the team wants outside customers to reach an internal server at a stable public address without renumbering the entire internal network.

Network Address Translation (NAT) solves both problems: it lets many internally-addressed devices share a small number of public IP addresses for outbound access, and lets specific internal servers be reachable at a fixed public address for inbound access — without either side needing to change its own addressing scheme.
concept: NAT is the process of rewriting IP address (and often port) information in a packet's header as it crosses a boundary — almost always the boundary between a private, internally-addressed network and the public internet. It is defined in RFC 1631 (updated by RFC 3022), and it exists specifically because of IPv4 address exhaustion, working hand-in-hand with the private address ranges reserved in RFC 1918:

2.1 The three classic types Type Mapping Typical use Static NAT One private IP ↔ one public IP, fixed, always the same Publishing an internal server (e.g., a web server) at a stable public address Dynamic NAT Many private IPs ↔ a pool of public IPs, assigned on demand Rarely used today — needs almost as many public IPs as Dynamic pool size PAT (NAT Overload) Many private IPs ↔ one public IP, disambiguated by port number The default at nearly every home and enterprise internet edge PAT (Port Address Translation), also called NAT Overload, is the version almost everyone actually uses:
it is what lets an entire office share one public IP by giving each outbound connection its own temporary public port number.
deep: 3.1 Cisco's four address terms (worth memorizing exactly) Term Meaning Inside Local A device's real, private address as seen inside the network Inside Global That same device's translated, public-facing address as seen from outside Outside Global The real public address of a destination out on the internet Outside Local How that outside destination's address appears from inside the network (usually Term Meaning identical to Outside Global, unless outside NAT is also in play) 3.2 The translation table For PAT, the NAT device maintains a translation table keyed on the full flow tuple — protocol, inside local IP:port, and the destination IP:port — mapped to a chosen inside global IP:port. Because the mapping includes the destination, the same internal device can have many simultaneous translated sessions open to different destinations, all sharing the single public IP but using different port numbers to stay distinguishable.

A single public IPv4 address has roughly 64,511 usable TCP/UDP ports (out of the 65,536 total, after subtracting well-known/reserved ranges), which is the practical ceiling on how many simultaneous PAT sessions one public IP can support — a real constraint at very large branch offices or under port- exhausting attacks.

3.3 CGNAT and NAT64 At ISP scale, Carrier-Grade NAT (CGNAT) uses the same PAT mechanism but one layer further out — an ISP shares one public IP across many customers, often using the RFC 6598 100.64.0.0/10 shared address space between the customer and the ISP's own NAT layer, resulting in "double NAT" for the customer.

NAT64 is a distinct transition mechanism that translates between IPv6-only clients and IPv4-only servers, relevant as networks migrate toward IPv6 while much of the internet remains IPv4-reachable only.
4. Internal Workflow — PAT Step by Step 1. An internal host (Inside Local 192.168.1.10) sends a packet to a website (Outside Global 93.184.216.34) through the NAT router's inside interface.

2. The router checks its NAT table for an existing translation matching this flow; none exists yet, so it creates one, choosing an available port on its own public IP (Inside Global) — e.g., 203.0.113.5:41230.
3. The router rewrites the packet's source IP:port from 192.168.1.10:52144 to 203.0.113.5:41230 and forwards it out the outside interface.

4. The website's reply arrives addressed to 203.0.113.5:41230. The router looks up that exact IP:port in its NAT table, finds the matching entry, and rewrites the destination back to 192.168.1.10:52144.
5. The router forwards the reply to the original internal host, which never sees or needs to know its packets were translated at all.
6. The table entry is removed after the connection closes (TCP) or after an idle timeout (UDP/ICMP), freeing the port for reuse.
enterprise: Internet edge router or firewall — PAT for outbound internet access is applied for essentially every enterprise network, translating hundreds or thousands of internal devices to one or a small handful of public IPs.

Static NAT on a firewall (e.g., a Palo Alto Networks device, as used at FundedNext) — used for Destination NAT, publishing an internal service at a fixed public IP/port, and for Source NAT, controlling exactly which public IP a specific internal segment appears to use outbound.

Data center mergers and migrations — static NAT is frequently used as a stop-gap to bridge two networks with overlapping private address ranges (a very common real-world situation after a company acquisition) without an immediate, disruptive renumbering project.

Cloud gateways — AWS NAT Gateway, Azure NAT Gateway, and similar managed services provide the same PAT function for cloud-hosted private subnets that need outbound internet access without direct public IPs.
6. Dependencies — What NAT Needs Beneath It
IPv4 addressing and subnetting (Sessions 30–32) — NAT exists specifically to translate between private and public address spaces defined by these standards.

Routing (Session 29, 36) — the NAT device must already have a correct route to reach the internet on its outside interface, and internal devices must already route their internet-bound traffic toward the NAT device (commonly via a default route).
TCP/UDP port fields (Session 39, upcoming) — PAT specifically depends on the transport-layer port number to disambiguate flows; ICMP uses its Query ID field the same way for ping-style traffic.
7. Dependents — What Relies on or Is Affected by NAT
ACLs/Firewall rules (Session 38, upcoming) — the order of NAT and ACL processing on a device changes which IP addresses the ACL actually needs to match, a frequent source of misconfiguration.

VPN/IPsec (Sessions 45–46, upcoming) — standard IPsec ESP does not include a port field, so ESP traffic traversing a PAT device breaks unless NAT-Traversal (NAT-T) is used, which wraps ESP in UDP port 4500 specifically so PAT can translate it correctly.

VoIP/SIP — SIP embeds IP addresses and ports inside its application payload, not just the packet header, so plain NAT does not automatically fix them; this is why VoIP deployments often need Application Layer Gateways (ALGs) or SIP-aware NAT handling.

DNS — internal clients resolving a company's own public-facing domain name to an internal server sometimes need split-horizon DNS or NAT hairpinning (also called NAT loopback) so they can reach the server via the same public name/IP they'd use from outside.
security: NAT is not a firewall, even though it is very often mistaken for one. Its actual security-relevant behavior is a side effect: because PAT only creates a translation table entry in response to outbound traffic, unsolicited inbound connections generally have no matching entry and get dropped — but this is a consequence of how the state table works, not an access-control policy someone designed and can audit.

Static NAT deliberately punches a permanent, predictable hole for inbound traffic to a specific internal host — this must always be paired with real firewall rules restricting what is allowed to reach that hole, not left to NAT alone.

Address hiding via PAT provides a mild obscurity benefit (external scanners can't directly enumerate internal IPs) but should never be relied upon as the actual security boundary — that job belongs to a real firewall/ACL policy.

NAT table/port exhaustion can itself be a denial-of-service vector — an attacker or a misbehaving application opening excessive simultaneous connections can exhaust the available PAT ports on a shared public IP, blocking new connections for everyone behind it.
troubleshooting: Symptom Likely Cause Check Internal hosts can't reach the internet at all Missing or incorrect NAT inside/outside interface designation, or missing ACL matching internal subnet Verify ip nat inside / ip nat outside on correct interfaces; check the NAT access-list Intermittent outbound failures under heavy load PAT port pool exhaustion on a single public IP show ip nat translations count;

consider adding public IPs to the pool Inbound service unreachable from outside No static NAT / destination NAT rule, or ACL blocking the translated port Verify static NAT entry and confirm the firewall permits the specific inbound port IPsec VPN drops or won't establish through NAT ESP has no port field and does not survive plain PAT Enable NAT-Traversal (NAT-T, UDP 4500) on both VPN endpoints Two merging networks can't communicate; addresses look identical Overlapping private subnets on both sides (e.g., both using 192.168.1.0/24) Deploy static NAT / twice-NAT to translate one or both sides to non- overlapping ranges Cisco IOS commands worth memorizing: show ip nat translations (the live table), show ip nat statistics (hits, active translations, pool usage), and clear ip nat translation * (to flush stuck entries during troubleshooting).
example: A branch office of 200 staff sits behind a single public IP from the ISP. The edge router runs PAT (ip nat inside source list 1 interface GigabitEthernet0/1 overload), translating every internal 192.168.10.0/24 address to that one public IP with a unique port per session — comfortably within the roughly 64,000- port ceiling for normal office use.

Separately, the same company publishes an internal web application to customers using static NAT: ip nat inside source static 192.168.10.50 203.0.113.20, mapping one specific internal server to one fixed public IP, paired with a firewall rule permitting only TCP/443 inbound to that address — NAT provides the address translation, the firewall provides the actual access control.
cloud: AWS NAT Gateway / Azure NAT Gateway / GCP Cloud NAT — fully-managed services that give private-subnet cloud instances outbound-only internet access without assigning them public IPs, functionally identical in concept to on-prem PAT.

Cloud load balancers perform Destination NAT (DNAT), rewriting a single public-facing IP/port into whichever backend instance's private IP should actually handle the request — conceptually the cloud-native evolution of on-prem static/destination NAT.

Kubernetes uses NAT internally as a core mechanism — kube-proxy commonly implements Services via iptables or IPVS rules that perform SNAT/DNAT to route traffic to the right backend Pod, invisible to the application but built on exactly the concepts in this session.

A genuinely important trend to know for interviews: IPv6's enormous address space removes the original scarcity problem that made NAT necessary, so IPv6-only cloud and enterprise designs increasingly avoid NAT for address-conservation purposes — though NAT66/NPTv6 still exists for other reasons like renumbering flexibility or multihoming.
automation: Terraform/CloudFormation provision NAT Gateways and their route-table associations declaratively as part of standard cloud network infrastructure-as-code.

Ansible modules (e.g., cisco.ios.ios_config, or vendor-specific Palo Alto Panorama modules) push standardized NAT policy templates across many edge devices, reducing the manual- misconfiguration risk highlighted in Section 9.
Monitoring scripts poll show ip nat statistics or cloud NAT Gateway metrics (e.g., AWS CloudWatch ErrorPortAllocation) to alert before port exhaustion causes an outage rather than after.

Firewall-as-code pipelines (common with Palo Alto's Panorama, relevant to FundedNext's stack) manage Source NAT and Destination NAT policies alongside security rules in version control, so NAT changes go through the same review process as any other firewall change.
career: Static NAT, Dynamic NAT, and PAT/NAT Overload configuration are explicit CCNA 200-301 exam topics, and the inside-local/inside-global/outside-local/outside-global terminology is a very common whiteboard-interview ask. Understanding why NAT-T exists for IPsec is a frequently-tested VPN troubleshooting scenario at both CCNA and real job-interview level.

This session connects directly to daily tooling relevant to the current role: Palo Alto Networks firewalls (part of FundedNext's stack) implement Source NAT and Destination NAT as first-class policy objects, so being fluent in NAT terminology and troubleshooting is directly transferable, practical knowledge for an infrastructure/security-adjacent role in that exact environment.
interview: Q1: What is the difference between NAT and PAT?

A: NAT (in the static/dynamic sense) maps IP addresses one-to-one or from a pool; PAT (NAT Overload) maps many private IPs to one public IP by additionally tracking port numbers, which is why it can support far more simultaneous internal hosts than public addresses.
Q2: Why does IPsec ESP traffic often fail to pass through a NAT device, and how is it fixed?

A: Standard ESP has no port field for PAT to rewrite, so the NAT device cannot properly track or translate ESP flows; NAT-Traversal (NAT-T) encapsulates ESP inside UDP (port 4500), giving PAT a port field to work with.
Q3: Explain Inside Local vs Inside Global.
A: Inside Local is a device's real private address as used inside the network; Inside Global is the translated public address that same device appears as when communicating outside the network.
Q4: Is NAT a security feature?

A: Not by design — its purpose is address translation. It has an incidental side effect of blocking unsolicited inbound connections in the PAT case, but real access control should come from firewall/ACL policy, not from NAT itself.
Q5: Two companies are merging and both use 192.168.1.0/24 internally. How would you handle it without an immediate renumbering project?
A: Deploy static NAT (or twice-NAT/double-NAT) at the interconnect point to translate one or both overlapping ranges into non-conflicting addresses until a permanent renumbering can be scheduled.

A: Generally no, for its original purpose — IPv6's address space is so large that address conservation isn't a driver — though a variant (NAT66/NPTv6) still exists for use cases like network renumbering flexibility or certain multihoming scenarios.
misconceptions: "NAT is a firewall." — False; NAT translates addresses, a firewall enforces access policy. They are frequently deployed on the same device but are different functions.
"NAT exists primarily to hide internal IPs for security." — Not accurate; NAT exists primarily to solve IPv4 address exhaustion. Address obscurity is a side effect, not the design goal.

"A network only ever gets NAT'd once." — False; double NAT (e.g., a home router behind an ISP's CGNAT) or even triple NAT is common and a frequent real-world cause of confusing connectivity issues, especially for gaming and self-hosted services.

"All traffic types work fine through PAT." — False; protocols that embed IP/port information inside their payload (like SIP) or that lack a port field (like plain ESP) need special handling (ALGs, NAT- T) to survive translation correctly.
"IPv6 eliminates the need for NAT entirely, everywhere." — Mostly true for address-conservation purposes, but not absolute; NAT66/NPTv6 use cases still exist.
anchors: Think of NAT as a company's front-desk receptionist and its single published phone number. Every employee (Inside Local) can call out, but to the outside world, every call appears to come from the same main office number (Inside Global) — the receptionist privately keeps a logbook (the NAT table) noting which employee's extension corresponds to which outbound call, so the return call gets routed to the right desk.

Static NAT is a direct-dial extension published on a business card — always rings the same desk. PAT is the shared switchboard number — endless outbound calls fit through it because the receptionist tracks each one by a temporary tag (port number).

Session 29 & 36 (Routing/Routing Protocols) — traffic must already be routed toward the NAT device before translation can happen; NAT does not replace routing.

19. Lab — Hands-On Environment: GNS3 or Packet Tracer with one Cisco IOS router acting as the internet edge, an internal LAN of 192.168.1.0/24, and a simulated "internet" host on the outside interface.
1. Designate interfaces: interface g0/0 → ip nat inside; interface g0/1 → ip nat outside.

2. Define which internal traffic is eligible for translation: access-list 1 permit 192.168.1.0 0.0.0.255 3. Enable PAT: ip nat inside source list 1 interface g0/1 overload 4. From an internal host, ping/traceroute the outside host, then run show ip nat translations on the router and confirm a translated entry appears with a unique port.
5. Generate several simultaneous sessions from different internal hosts and confirm each gets its own port under the same single public IP.
Part B — Static NAT (publishing a server):

1. Configure: ip nat inside source static 192.168.1.50 203.0.113.20 2. From the outside host, attempt to reach 203.0.113.20 and confirm it reaches the internal 192.168.1.50 server, then verify the fixed entry persists in show ip nat translations even with no active traffic (unlike a dynamic PAT entry, which times out).
